 Follow Localized cease-fire begins in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky
 Jill Keppeler Tue, October 27, 2026 at 6:32 PM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Ukrainian rescue workers carry a victim from a residential building in Kyiv, Ukraine, after it was struck by a Russian missile October 14. A localized cease-fire went into effect Tuesday in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where people have been trapped for years. Photo by Vlad Movchan/UPI Oct. 27 (UPI) -- A limited cease-fire started Tuesday in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, Ukraine, where people have been trapped without consistent access to food, water or electricity for years.
 Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian parliament commissioner for human rights, said in social media posts that the cease-fire went into effect at 3 a.m. and that, as of 5:30 p.m., both countries were adhering to the terms.
 He said the cease-fire was scheduled to remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. Sunday.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I hope that everything will continue in accordance with the agreed plan and that we will be able to help the civilians in Oleshky who are eagerly awaiting assistance," Lubinets wrote.
 Russia's defense ministry also said the cease-fire was under effect and that both sides are respecting it.
 Oleshky is on the front lines in Russia's invasion of Ukraine, with the Dnipro River on one side and Russia's forces on the other. Russia occupied it in the early days of the invasion in 2022, and getting supplies into the city has been difficult and dangerous, BBC News reported . Evacuation is likewise dangerous because of mines and drone attacks.
 Oleshky once had 24,000 citizens, but about 1,700 remain in the city, with up to 6,000 people in the greater area. The city has not had gas, electricity or water services for three years.
 Advertisement Advertisement During the cease-fire, forces are supposed to allow supplies in and enable safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday. However, details on the evacuation plans were unclear, BBC News reported, with many people worried that Russia will not allow them to return to Ukraine -- or will examine their phones for signs of Ukrainian support, which could result in imprisonment and torture.
 The White House has said the cease-fire was secured by first lady Melania Trump. Pope Leo XIV had also appealed to Russia to allow food and other aid into Oleshky.
 Trump said Tuesday that the cease-fire has expanded beyond Oleshky "within the Kherson Region" to provide passage for humanitarian convoys. Kherson is the largest Ukrainian city on the front line.
